Hornets star Knueppel sidelined by hamstring injury
The Charlotte Hornets announced that Kon Knueppel will be out for at least the entire preseason because of a left hamstring injury.

James: Maxey, Embiid were factors in joining 76ers
LeBron James said his longstanding friendship with All-Star Tyrese Maxey and a desire to help Joel Embiid win his first NBA title played significant roles in his decision to sign a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in July.

"[Embiid has] done everything in our league, and the only thing he has not done is win a championship. And I want to try to help him get that first one," James said. "He has a city on his back. He's been 'The Process' for 10 years, 12 years, however long he's been there. But I think it's time we even get you deeper into the process. And I hope that I can be, kind of, that final little piece that can help him get over the hump."

Grizzlies waive Russell
The Memphis Grizzlies have waived D'Angelo Russell, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Russell has made one All-Star team during his career and was selected No. 2 in the 2015 NBA draft.

stories.headline: State of each position in 2026: What are the biggest tactical trends?
stories.summary: Elite soccer has changed dramatically in recent years, and the most valued player skill sets have evolved as a result.
stories.body:
Elite European soccer in 2026 feels decidedly different from what we've become used to. Over the past couple of seasons, the Premier League has been increasingly characterized by direct attacking, set pieces and long throw-ins. Many encounters between big clubs across Europe have become frenetic, end-to-end affairs, such as the Bayern Munich-Paris Saint-Germain semifinals in last season's UEFA Champions League.

A lot of the changes seem related to how teams play without the ball. The soccer we became accustomed to throughout the 2010s involved top sides trying to push their opponents back while keeping the ball. Once the ball reached the attacking third, they tried to outnumber defenders in key spaces and make use of their attacking talent.

One way for defensive sides to counter this approach is to use zonal marking, which involves defending space rather than individual players. They would set up in compact blocks and deny space in critical areas, whether they defended deep like Max Allegri's Juventus in the 2010s or pressed high like teams coached by Ralf Rangnick's disciples. While this tactic helps protect the areas closer to goal and prevent mismatches, it sometimes plays into the hands of those high-possession sides.

As a result, player marking (or man-to-man marking), in which defenders are assigned to follow attackers around up and down the pitch, started to make a comeback at the turn of the 2020s. Teams like Mikel Arteta's Arsenal and Andoni Iraola's Bournemouth combined this concept with their zonal marking, switching out of a zonal structure in certain situations to swarm teams attempting to move the ball forward (hybrid pressing). This makes moving the ball slowly up the pitch harder, causing teams to embrace more direct approaches with the ball.

Meanwhile, the game appears to be becoming more physical and more intense. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, every passing season of the Premier League has seen faster sprinting and more "high-intensity actions." And with off-ball physical data like running distance or top speed becoming more accessible, scouting departments now possess more transparent measures of athleticism, leading to players' athletic qualities being valued more.

Rather than just affecting the head coach's team talk, these big-picture changes have a major effect on the skill sets that clubs look for when assembling their starting XIs. Let's take a look at five positions -- goalkeepers, center backs, fullbacks, central midfielders, and strikers -- to see what has changed and why.

Goalkeepers: Distribution and cross-claiming

New Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki has generated much buzz this season. One of his standout features has been his passing ability, playing quick passes to his center backs during the early buildup and exquisite floated long passes to Villa's forwards to escape pressure.

As impressive as his reflex saves are, Suzuki doesn't appear to be a great shot stopper. His "goals prevented" stats, based on post-shot expected goals, reveal that his shot-stopping numbers have hovered around that of the average major league goalkeeper over the past couple of seasons. In fact, in 2025-26, he prevented minus-0.4 goals per 90 minutes, implying that he did slightly worse than the average keeper last season.

However, his passing displays and his excellent cross-claiming make him a highly prized player, and his skill set epitomizes the state of today's goalkeeping.

When Pep Guardiola's Manchester City signed Gianluigi Donnarumma -- known for his shot-stopping abilities, but arguably an average distributor -- as their first-choice goalkeeper in summer 2025, it looked like elite soccer was once again prioritizing shot-stopping between the sticks. But the tactical conditions of soccer in the 2020s make ball-playing goalkeepers even more crucial than before; when teams are tasked with playing the ball past intense man-to-man presses, goalkeepers have more to do in the buildup phase.

Even the most aggressive man-to-man presses don't generally mark the goalkeeper, making keepers free options in the buildup. From this point, keepers are instrumental to playing quick passes around the box to try to bait the press for "artificial transitions" as well as with playing longer passes into space to relieve pressure and kick-start a direct attack.

As a result, the heyday of keepers primarily known for what they can do with their feet looks unlikely to recede anytime soon, with more intense pressing and more direct attacking arguably magnifying their value.

Meanwhile, although the number of open-play crosses that teams in the Big Five leagues play has decreased slightly since 2018, the ever-rising threat of set-play goals makes cross-claiming an especially valuable skill. The first-choice keepers at big clubs dominate the top of the leaderboard for cross-claiming statistics; Donnarumma ranked No. 1 for the highest percentage of crosses claimed in the Premier League last season, Barcelona's Joan García and Real Madrid's Thibaut Courtois ranked second and third, respectively, in last season's LaLiga campaign, and PSG's Lucas Chevalier ranked third in Ligue 1.

On the other hand, the keepers who populated the bottom of cross-claiming tables belong to either lower-table clubs or underperforming established sides like Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United. As valuable as goalkeepers' distribution is in 2026, it appears that the ability to claim crosses has become crucial to success between the sticks.

Center backs: Playmaking and pushing forward

In the 2015-16 Premier League season, the top five players who completed the most passes per 90 were Santi Cazorla, Cesc Fabregas, Bastian Schweinsteiger, Aaron Ramsey and Michael Carrick, with more central and attacking midfielders completing the top 10. In 2025-26, the top five were Rodri, Lewis Dunk, Curtis Jones, Trevoh Chalobah and William Saliba, with seven center backs making up the top 10.

A decade ago, central midfielders were at the heart of elite sides' passing moves, but today, especially in the Premier League, center backs are the primary passers in most sides.

In the Big Five leagues, center backs completed 19% more passes in the 2025-26 season than in 2018-19. Much of this has to do with intense man-to-man pressing systems, meaning that players positioned deeper have more prominent buildup duties. The 2020s have also seen nominal center backs become more involved in attacking play, taking up higher and wider positions. Attacking center backs are effective tools to dismantle mid-blocks, helping complicate marking duties with their movement.

This is easiest to do with wide center backs in a back three. Gian Piero Gasperini's Atalanta and Simone Inzaghi's Internazionale did this especially often. This season, Xabi Alonso's Chelsea and Gasperini's AS Roma are key examples, with the latter probably representing the most adventurous iteration of attacking center backs we've seen this century.

We can see some of this in back-four systems, too. Guardiola used John Stones as a center back who roved forward in possession at City, while Thiago Motta used Riccardo Calafiori and Jhon Lucumí as center backs with free roles.

As this decade progresses, the phrase "center back" might be encased in quotation marks more often.

Fullbacks: Rise of the underlap

Fullbacks often epitomize the tactical eras they find themselves in. The turn of the 2010s saw the rise of overlapping attacking fullbacks who move high up the pitch and outside wingers who cut inside with the ball. The mid-to-late 2010s saw the rise of high-intensity pressing, with high-possession sides using inverted fullbacks to provide security against counterattacks resulting from losing the ball. Meanwhile, the relative conservatism that followed the COVID-19 pandemic meant that nominal center backs were often deployed at fullback.

Today, we're seeing the rise of attacking fullbacks who underlap, making runs into the channels between opposition fullbacks and center backs, much like inverted wingers. As Caleb Gearty notes for SCOUTED, "the ability to receive the ball" is progressively becoming more highly valued for fullbacks. After getting in behind back lines, underlapping fullbacks can put in dangerous cutbacks and crosses from closer to goal, or take shots themselves.

In the case of back-three formations, this isn't a new phenomenon. For instance, Thomas Tuchel's Chelsea saw wingbacks Reece James and Ben Chilwell move inside and score goals, while Inzaghi used Federico Dimarco and Denzel Dumfries as goal-scoring threats at Inter.

But now, fullbacks in back-four systems are increasingly venturing forward and inside -- not just putting crosses in, but getting on the end of goal-scoring opportunities, too. Arsenal's Calafiori and Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly often make darting runs into the box and offer secondary goal threats. Spain's World Cup win saw Marc Cucurella and Pedro Porro underlap, pulling defenses apart.

Meanwhile, back-three systems feature wingbacks who pose greater goal-scoring threats than ever. Alonso's Chelsea are an instructive example -- they signed Pep Chavarría and Marco Palestra, but Alonso currently appears to favor the left-footed winger Pedro Neto at right wingback, who makes sharp runs into the box.

Why is this the case? In an age when defensive tactics are dominated by player-marking, the positional interchanges around the flanks (or "wide rotations") and unexpected diagonal darts forward from fullbacks can scramble player-marking duties and open up space -- especially when wingers find themselves closer to the sideline. As Billy Carpenter writes, sudden moves into the spaces in behind defenses can expose structural vulnerabilities in even the best mid-blocks.

Calafiori so far this season represents a great example, making well-timed runs in behind and receiving incisive through balls ...

... and creating goals like these.

Jamie Carragher once remarked that fullbacks are either failed wingers or failed center backs. The rise of inverted fullbacks would've allowed Carragher to add "failed midfielder" to his jibe, while today, a middling inside forward can consider a successful career as an underlapping attacking fullback.

Central midfielders: Large spaces and generalists

In 2026, the most expensive player archetype to sign in soccer appears to be the generalist midfielder. Of the 10 most expensive transfers this summer per Transfermarkt, six were central midfielders. And among the major moves in midfield that big clubs made this summer, most midfielders are do-it-all generalists who, at least in theory, contribute to passing, carrying, winning the ball back and sometimes crashing the box. These include Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Bruno Guimarães, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos.

This hasn't always been the case. By 2009, the box-to-box midfielder had become a dying breed, superseded by specialists in midfield. In the late 2010s, the rise of pressing meant that press-resistant ball carriers in midfield became increasingly valued, epitomized by the summer 2019 transfer window, which saw Frenkie de Jong, Tanguy Ndombele and Mateo Kovacic move for sums exceeding €40 million. But now, every big club is willing to spend astronomic sums on their own equivalent of Declan Rice or Moisés Caicedo; athletic midfielders who can cover lots of ground and do a bit of everything.

Counterintuitively, this might be happening because less of the game is happening in midfield. With the rise of situational player-marking, the middle third sees larger spaces opened up between lines of pressure, while space becomes more constricted in teams' own thirds. As a result, moving the ball from defense to midfield becomes a harder task, while the spaces opened up in the middle third mean teams don't pass the ball around as much there, instead moving the ball through it more quickly.

Jon Mackenzie and Jake Entwistle have discussed the relevance of "small spaces" -- where the player on the ball has little room to work with in the face of pressure -- and "large spaces" -- where players need to cover ground quickly, especially during transitions or when a line of pressure is broken -- in midfield, which influences how midfielder profiles are valued today. A player like Anderson, who combines small-space and large-space skills, becomes priceless, but the broader emphasis shifts from small-space specialists to large-space generalists who can cover ground and offer control in the center of the park.

As a result, affecting the pace of the attack, rather than just exerting control over space, becomes a key consideration in midfield. The rise of artificial transitions in response to pressing also means central midfielders are key to moving the ball from small spaces to large spaces, as Carlos Baleba did adeptly while at Brighton.

The middle of the park is integral to controlling a game of soccer, and as we're seeing the very notion of "control" change in the middle of the 2020s, the traits associated with the most highly valued midfielders are transformed, too.

Strikers: Physicality and pinning

While the first two decades of top-level soccer in the 21st century saw increasing versatility at the center forward position, the opposite is happening in the third decade. So far, the 2020s have seen taller, faster and stronger strikers being valued more than their smaller, more technical counterparts. Of course, Erling Haaland represents the platonic ideal of a striker -- in this era and in any other -- but the players who spearhead attacks in the middle of the 2020s tend to be 6-foot-2 or taller, and combine their size with pace.

Today's strikers are also less involved in link-up play than their equivalents at the turn of the 2020s, with the average striker in the Big Five leagues completing 16% fewer passes in 2025-26 than in 2018-19.

As discussed earlier, with attacks becoming more direct, the established strategy of pushing teams back and overwhelming defenses with patient play in the attacking third is falling out of fashion, which means strikers don't need to be as involved outside the penalty area. Instead, strikers increasingly spend most of the game pinning back defenders and stretching back lines, attempting to find space within settled defensive blocks. Plus, an increased emphasis on transitions correspondingly makes outlets to hit on the break becoming more valuable, and some extra size certainly comes in handy while trying to score goals from set pieces.

However, the players who currently lead most big clubs' front lines indicate the trend might be reversing at the upper echelons of the game. Harry Kane drops deeper than ever and conducts passing moves from midfield at Bayern, PSG won the Champions League with Ousmane Dembélé as a false 9 last season, Mikel Arteta appears to favor Kai Havertz up front over Viktor Gyokeres at Arsenal, and Barcelona currently deploy Raphinha at the No. 9 spot.

This might be because teams are finding alternate ways of manipulating player-marking strategies, picking holes in defenses with positional interchanges. By dropping deeper, a striker can bring the defender assigned to marking him along and create space for teammates. For example, in this case, João Pedro dropping deep to receive a throw-in pokes a hole for Morgan Rogers to run into, who in turn creates space for Cole Palmer's carry and goal.

For now, specialized, physically gifted strikers may have their time in the sun, but we're likely to see many approaches at the center forward position as the decade progresses.

What to make of 2026 trends

Many soccer fans view today's tactical landscape as being one of stasis or even regression. It's tempting to view the rise of directness and set pieces, as well as do-it-all midfielders and big strikers, as the return of older approaches. But this might be a reductive view; as Mackenzie notes in his book "The Spectre of Pep," presenting changes in the tactical landscape as purely being "cyclical" makes it "very difficult to speak of the 'new' in any meaningful way at all."

All the smaller tactical shifts we're seeing across the pitch are happening in relation to broader changes in the tactical environment of the 2020s. With the rise of man-to-man pressing approaches and the resulting revival of direct attacking, accompanied with the resurgence of ground-eating midfielders and big, physical strikers, these very same trends have brought about the rise of playmaking goalkeepers, attacking center backs, and underlapping fullbacks.

If a Premier League manager from 2006 drove a plutonium-powered DeLorean to 2026, he might find the first five minutes of play recognizable, but would be scandalized by the time he reaches the 10-minute mark. Welcome to elite soccer in the 2020s.

stories.headline: Could Malaysia return to F1 calendar? The state of play despite Sepang travel chaos
stories.summary: Malaysia's Sepang circuit hosted a popular -- and, as it stands, one-off -- return to the Formula 1 calendar, although it was overshadowed by three days of travel chaos and nightmare experiences for fans.
stories.body:
Malaysia's Sepang circuit hosted a popular -- and, as it stands, one-off -- return to the Formula 1 calendar, although it was overshadowed by three days of travel chaos and nightmare experiences for fans.

The race itself delivered an entertaining spectacle full of incident, albeit after a demonstration of the worst part of F1's new V6 turbo hybrid engines. So where has its stand-in appearance as the Bahrain Grand Prix left it in terms of returning in the future?

After the race, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim confirmed discussions with F1 about the likelihood of the nation becoming a regular F1 host again.

"Had the opportunity to hold a meeting with the President who also serves as the Chief Executive Officer of Formula 1, Stefano Domenicali, before the race began at the Sepang International Circuit," he posted on X. "We discussed the prospects of reinstating the Malaysia Grand Prix permanently in the Formula 1 calendar, thereby fulfilling the long-standing desire of fans who have eagerly awaited its return to Sepang. However, this effort will require time because arranging the race calendar must take into account the packed schedule as well as existing contractual commitments with host countries."

- Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires

- Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet

- George Russell on Bahrain GP retirement: 'Beyond disappointment' as title chances all but over

Sources with knowledge of the calendar have told ESPN that any deal with Sepang will be a long way off as things stand, but there is clearly renewed energy behind the circuit's viability as a race host. F1 boss Domenicali often says there's a long waiting list of venues who are hoping to get an event of their own and he's not wrong.

Sources have told ESPN Sepang has put itself into Formula 1's good graces by accommodating the Bahrain event -- which will help the sport keep its commercial obligation of not dropping below 22 events in 2026 -- but that also does not mean it has automatically shot to the top of any waiting or priority list

One well-placed paddock source told ESPN that, given the current F1 deals in existence, the earliest Sepang could come back to the race calendar would be 2030, a timeline Sepang officials would not confirm or deny when asked on record. The official line all weekend, until the prime minister's comments, that all focus was on the 2026 event. But a lot needs to happen for any deal beyond that to gather pace.

Finances will be the biggest obstacle. Bahrain stumped up most if not all of the reported $50 million hosting fee for this year's event. Without that, there's no chance Sepang could have been a 2027 fallback option, it wasn't sat around with a bucketload of cash just waiting for an opportunity to host a race if needed.The venue dropped off the calendar in 2017 because it could not afford F1's hosting fees as they were then -- an influx of new races this side of the pandemic has escalated the average fee even more, with F1 enjoying a commercial boom it has never experienced before.

But one thing was clear from Sunday's event: the appetite for the sport in Malaysia is bigger than ever. A lack of fan interest in a fallow time for F1 killed the event off a decade ago: demand appears to be well and truly back now and that might help the circuit in its bid to find the financial backing it would need to even have a shot at having a seat at the table in future.

Why was the fan experience so bad?

One of the standout moments ​of Sepang's weekend was the loud roar from the fans when Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton made crucial passes during the race -- Malaysia's fanbase was always loud and over 110,000 people were in attendance for raceday alone.

Many of them will have endured a lot to have seen those overtakes.

Because Sepang's event was the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Bahrain's race organisers took control of all elements of the event -- it flew in meat for the paddock, local ice cream vendors, over 500 event marshals, and even organised its Gulf Air Dreamliner to fly over the grid (even in the middle of a deluge of rain) to keep its prerace tradition alive. It was the equivalent of someone leasing out a friend's house for a party, but telling them they would deal with every single facet of the event.

The fact that it was Bahrain and not Malaysia involved in planning every detail, plus the number of people in attendance, caused problems.

- Lewis Hamilton: No plans to visit casino with Ferrari strategists after slick tyre gamble

- Max Verstappen praises Red Bull on 'very special' Bahrain Grand Prix win after 'tough start to year'

"We're not used to this," Bahrain International Circuit chief executive Sheikh Salman bin Isa Al Khalifa told ESPN ahead of the weekend. "It's not like we have experience in those numbers."

Bahrain's infrastructure is usually built around an event which caters for 55,000 fans a day, but the attendance was double that every day. The grandstand along the start-finish line alone held 35,000 fans. Bahraini officials were not only dealing with a completely unfamiliar circuit and external road system but an influx of fans they simply do not deal with at their Sakhir equivalent.

Anyone travelling into the circuit could see that the people organising this year's event were overwhelmed. From Friday onwards, there were reports of fans having to walk up to 11 kilometers home because shuttles had simply stopped without warning immediately after sessions finished. ESPN saw hoards of people walking down the motorway's hard shoulder on all three days of the event, noticeably at its worst on Friday but bad every day.

Things compounded the problem, like the Grab and Bolt exclusion zone stopping rideshare companies from getting anywhere near the venue. Once fans got into the venue, they found progress getting anywhere slow. Queues for grandstand gates were slow, queues for concessions stands even slower.

F1 photographer Kym Illman extensively covered the chaos within the circuit on his video channels -- he reported plastic water bottles being banned on entry (fans then had to buy bottled water inside the venue) and long lines of up to an hour for water refill stations, many of which ran out of water early in the event, and there were reports of 50 ambulances being sent into the circuit on Friday alone for people who had passed out in the humid conditions.

Videos from Saturday's DJ Axwell concert on Saturday -- in a field which was supposed to accommodate 10,000 people -- had upwards of 50,000 people in attendance, with many leaving the venue either during qualifying or immediately after qualifying having heard horror stories from the day before. It caused an almighty bottleneck outside the circuit and many fans were left stranded in no man's land -- unable to get anywhere, but also not allowed to return inside the circuit -- for hours on end in the stifling Malaysia heat.

This appeared to have caused similar on Sunday, with various reports on social media of fans leaving before the end of the race to try and avoid similar chaos, but still getting back to their hotels 10 or 11 hours later. It all left a sour taste for many and overshadowed what was otherwise a popular return for one of F1's great venues of its more recent past.

Who was to blame was an open question -- many in attendance pointed the finger at Bahrain's organisers, who appeared to have underestimated the logistical challenge of putting on a race at a venue many of them had never visited before, but the eight-week turnaround from the announcement to the event did not help.

Sources have told ESPN that F1 would have intervened and made tweaks to basic things such as motorway signage had there been more time to properly come up with a plan of action -- most events are meticulously planned and mapped out for months in advance, and many of them do not go ahead without problems anyway. Local Malaysian police also seemed slightly overwhelmed by the amount of traffic outside the circuit, especially on Friday and Saturday.

That might all be simplified should Sepang host the event itself in future -- the venue regularly holds a MotoGP event without similar issues and it seems as though a perfect storm of things contributed to the bad time a lot of fans experienced across the three days.

stories.headline: MLB 2026 playoffs: Ranking home-field advantage for every team
stories.summary: From atmosphere to unique structures, some places are harder to play than others. Here are the clubs who benefit the most.
stories.body:
Tony Gwynn Jr. grew up going to games at Jack Murphy Stadium when his father, Tony Gwynn, played for the San Diego Padres, and he played in Petco Park himself during his own eight-year MLB career, so he has seen the dramatic evolution of the ballpark atmosphere in San Diego.

"What flies under the radar is that with the departure of the [NFL's] Chargers, this opened space for more fanatic Padres fans," Gwynn Jr. wrote in a text to ESPN. "This generation of Padre fans seems to be more fanatical than the generation I came up watching, when the fans could kind of take it or leave it. With the Padres being the only team in town now, it's just a different type of fan than it was before."

That the experience at a Padres games for fans and players -- on both teams -- has changed is indisputable. What is debatable is where Petco Park ranks in terms of home-field advantage among the eight teams still alive in the division series and battling for a World Series title.

We spoke to a number of managers and coaches -- who, of course, have all competed in the ballparks still in play -- on home-field advantage among the remaining clubs to create this ranking, based on their years of experience and feedback.

1. Yankee Stadium, New York Yankees

When the Yankees moved from their old home to the new Yankee Stadium in 2009, the initial narrative was that the new place didn't have the soul of the old place, because the new Yankee Stadium seemed bigger and more cavernous, with less intensity. But most of those we polled contend that the current Yankee Stadium provides the best home-field advantage in these playoffs.

"The combination of the crowd, the atmosphere, all of the postseason history," one NL staffer said.

"It's still the gold standard for a home field," an AL staffer said. "The fans are there early. They are loud. Their passion can be felt from Pitch 1. The event feels different. It still has the edge that impacts the opponent."

The atmosphere at Yankee Stadium has affected opposing teams in the past. During the 2017 playoffs, the Houston Astros were swept in the middle three games they played in New York of their best-of-seven ALCS. After Game 5, Houston's Carlos Beltran called a meeting, believing that his teammates were being impacted by Yankee Stadium's atmosphere, and told them they needed to calm down.

2. Petco Park, San Diego Padres

One AL staffer wrote in a text, "Petco is most improved and arguably 1-B to Yankee Stadium. The music, the vibe, the volume all impact the visiting team. The in-game is noticeably on point. The fans are all-in. It is no longer a chill place."

Nope, it is not. Due to the Western Metal Building in left field that looms over the field and the low outfield fencing, fans seem to be right on top of the players, making the whole place play like a small ballpark. But it's not small. With the expanded Gallagher Square seating, it can hold 47,000-plus fans, team president Erik Greupner said. San Diego was second in home attendance this past regular season, with 3.35 million, ranking behind only ... our next team.

3. Dodger Stadium, Los Angeles Dodgers

The Dodgers' players themselves make this a difficult place for visitors, of course, with the collection of future Hall of Famers comprising the lineup and the accomplished starting pitchers. But what was cited the most by rival staffers was the noise.

"Loud," one of the staffers said. "The speakers are incredible. The fan base is amazing."

"It's just so loud there," another said. "It's like the bass from the speakers thumps you in the chest."

4. Tropicana Field, Tampa Bay Rays

A long list of factors was cited by those polled as they addressed the difficulty for teams visiting St. Petersburg, from the inherent distraction of the nearby beaches to the way that the fan noise ricochets in the park. Most often mentioned, however, was the artificial surface and the enormous outfield, and how the Rays' team is custom built for its park, with speed (Chandler Simpson) and a pitching staff that fills the strike zone to take advantage of the spacious dimensions.

"The fast surface always matches their offensive style," one AL staffer said. "The goal has always been to not get swept there."

5. Truist Park, Atlanta Braves
Some of the staffers polled mentioned the enthusiasm of Braves fans, as well as their collective volume. A couple of them mentioned how hot it can get -- which has been the case already. When the forecast for Game 1 of the NLDS called for triple-digit temperatures, Atlanta manager Walt Weiss dismissed the impact, saying his team was accustomed to playing in that kind of weather.

6. American Family Field, Milwaukee Brewers
Brewers fans show up early and stay late, and when Jackson Chourio smashed the walk-off single to beat Padres closer Mason Miller and secure the Game 2 win, those fans shared in the sort of moment that will be remembered beyond this generation. The place was bonkers.

But the managers and coaches who responded in this poll are accustomed to noisy fans. What they find most difficult about playing in Milwaukee are the late-afternoon shadows and the working conditions. One staffer said that the clubhouse, food and batting cage are all the worst in the league, "so that makes it tougher to play there."

7. Progressive Field, Cleveland Guardians

"It's not an intimidating place for us," one staffer said. "Maybe that's because they typically have a lot of young players. They have good teams, but there's nothing that makes it a tough place to play. Not compared to some of the other places, certainly."

8. Rate Field, Chicago White Sox
"It's a neutral for me," one NL staffer said. "Nothing really stands out."

The growing popularity of the pope hats -- and the improvement of the White Sox, from setting the modern MLB single-season loss record in 2024 with 121 losses to making the playoffs and winning their first series since 2005 -- might start to change that.

stories.headline: UFC 332 takeaways: Talbott, Silva validate their top billing
stories.summary: Payton Talbott finished another former champion in Deiveson Figueiredo on a night full of knockouts at UFC 332.
stories.body:
The options were plenty for performance bonuses after UFC 332 in Salt Lake City. The fight card set a UFC record for knockouts with 11, and nine came in the first round. The most resounding KO went to men's bantamweight Payton Talbott in the co-main event. He came out strong, sending former champion Deiveson Figueiredo to the canvas twice before finishing him a little over two minutes into the fight. The win is Talbott's second in a row over a former champion and likely means big things ahead for him, but the loss for Figueiredo doesn't do anything to minimize his legacy in the UFC.

The main event, which received prefight chatter over whether it was worthy of a headlining slot, was high energy but mostly one-sided. Natalia Silva, the No. 1 women's flyweight contender, earned her first UFC championship with a unanimous decision over Wang Cong. The 29-year-old joins men's flyweight Joshua Van as the only UFC champions under 30.

Was the main event criticism validated?
The UFC took heat on social media for booking Silva vs. Wang in a main event on a numbered card. Silva was at the front of a long line of women's flyweight title contenders, no question, but it's fair to say Wang, unranked by ESPN and outside the top five in the UFC's own rankings, jumped the queue.

But while I'm on board with a lot of the criticism the UFC receives for its matchmaking, especially at a championship level, I understand what the fight promotion was going for in this case: The UFC was trying to set up a couple of possible storylines involving Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the women's flyweight title to make the Silva-Wang title fight a possibility after suffering an undisclosed injury that will sideline her for "up to one year."

Why Wang? She might not have an extensive UFC résumé, but she beat Shevchenko in a kickboxing match in 2015. Their history is not unlike that of Alex Pereira and Israel Adesanya, who met twice in kickboxing, with Pereira winning both and knocking out Adesanya in one of those fights. It provided a setup for their UFC rivalry.

A Wang vs. Shevchenko angle became moot, as things turned out, because Silva was too much for the Chinese fighter to handle. Wang came in with a 10-1 MMA record, but she had zero fights against top-10 flyweights, and it showed. Silva, by contrast, came in having defeated former UFC champions (Jessica Andrade, Alexa Grasso and Rose Namajunas) in each of her past three fights.

Silva was too fast, too elusive and too precise with her punches and kicks. Wang had no answers, looked lost and couldn't get her offense going until the fifth round, when it was too late. Not to vindicate the prefight matchmaking criticism, but this sure was a lopsided and not-so-fiery bout, one that got booed by a crowd that had been treated to a UFC-record 11 knockouts on the night.

So now the 125-pound division is left with the Silva vs. Shevchenko storyline we were expecting to see before Shevchenko was injured. It will be interesting to see how Silva's speed holds up when she meets her predecessor with the belt, and how differently she'll fight when up against an opponent with a strong grappling game. Oddly, that wasn't even addressed in Silva's postfight interview in the cage. Shevchenko's name wasn't even mentioned. Now, that is a UFC decision worth questioning. -- Jeff Wagenheim

Quick thanks to Figueiredo

MMA loves to move quickly, and it's ready to move very fast with Talbott. Talbott is everything MMA could want in a prospect, and his future is very bright.

So before we all take off on the Talbott train (as we inevitably will), let's take a moment to shout out one of the most exciting flyweights of all time, Figueiredo.

Let's be honest, Figueiredo was always a borrowed bantamweight. He struggled to make 125 pounds, and most of the sport was happy to see him ditch the weight cut in 2023, but he was also undersized at 135.

It's easy to forget now, as UFC men's flyweight champion Van has taken the sport by storm -- but the flyweight division was still in a precarious position when Figueiredo made his mark in 2020. Henry Cejudo saved the division by knocking out TJ Dillashaw in 2018, but then eventually vacated a weight class the UFC seriously considered shutting down. Figueiredo picked up where Cejudo left off, saving the division with his one-punch knockout power and (frankly) villain charisma. He played the role of "bad guy" in his back-to-back fights against Joseph Benavidez in 2020, as well as his four-fight rivalry with Brandon Moreno.

It was inevitable when he moved up in weight, but for a three-year period, Figueiredo was the exact figure the flyweight division needed. The 38-year-old's career is undoubtedly coming to an end soon, but Figueiredo was not just a terrific fighter and champion in his prime, he will forever be remembered as a significant hero of flyweight MMA. -- Brett Okamoto

stories.headline: Lacob lauds Williams as world's best after Valkyries' Game 1 win
stories.summary: Gabby Williams scored 25 points and played lockdown defense in a performance that led Valkyries owner Joe Lacob to declare her the "best player in the world."
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Golden State Valkyries owner Joe Lacob walked through the tunnels of Chase Center following the Valkyries' 71-60 win over the Las Vegas Aces in Game 1 of the WNBA semifinals with a message he wanted to get off of his chest.

"Print this: Gabby Williams is the best player in the world," Lacob told ESPN.

Williams scored a team-high 25 points Sunday afternoon and scored or assisted on 36 of the Valkyries' points. On the other end, she held the Aces to just 29% on 4-of-14 shooting as the primary defender. Williams, who also had 11 rebounds and five assists, became the second player with 25 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a playoff game against the Aces. She is also the first Valkyries player to have a 25-10-5 playoff game.

After arriving in Golden State during the offseason, Williams has taken her play to another level with the Valkyries -- finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and also adding to her offensive game. So far, she's averaging 25 points during the playoffs, which is the third-highest scoring average of the postseason. Only Wilson and Arike Ogunbowale have scored more.

Early in the game Sunday, Williams felt that the Aces were trying to make her uncomfortable, throwing a mixture of coverages at her. That's when she made sure she was intentional about getting everyone else involved.

"There are five players on the court," Williams said. "We were running really well in transition, so I found [Kayla Thornton] a couple times, and things started to open up on their own."

The Valkyries' ability to get out and run was fueled by their performance on the boards. Golden State outrebounded Las Vegas 52-25 -- the second-largest difference by any team in a playoff game in WNBA history. It also held the Aces to a season low in scoring.

The Aces made pushes, clawing back from down by as much as 11, but they never took away Golden State's momentum and couldn't get their deficit below five points down the stretch of the game.

"All we talked about the last 48 hours was rebounding and blocking them out, and we did not do that. Period," Aces coach Becky Hammon said. "The good news is, we played like ass and only lost by 10."

A'ja Wilson finished with 24 points on 8-of-21 field goal shooting and went 8-of-11 from the free throw line. Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young combined for 25 points.

"I've competed against A'ja my entire career, and she will go down in history as the best player to ever do it," Williams said. "This is what you dream about. You dream to play against players like that. Going up against them is all I care about. ... I just want to win."

Williams rolled her eyes when she heard what Lacob said about her, but the belief he has poured into her is the reason she is leading the Valkyries in their playoff push. During every game, she seeks out a fist bump from the owner to "absorb" some of his energy. When she watches replays of the game, she zooms in to see his spirited reaction to big plays.

"There she is," Lacob yelled when he saw Williams standing in the hallway after the game, his arms open for a hug. "Best player in the world. No one is saying it, but they need to start saying it."

stories.headline: Merrett moves to Hawks as Bombers avoid ugly trade war
stories.summary: Zach Merrett can breath a sigh of relief, with the former Essendon captain headed to Hawthorn after the bitter AFL rivals agreed to a trade.
stories.body:
Zach Merrett can breath a sigh of relief, with the former Essendon captain headed to Hawthorn after the bitter AFL rivals agreed to a trade.

Hawthorn and Essendon locked in a deal for the 31-year-old on Monday afternoon, hours after the AFL trade window opened.

The Hawks will give up picks No.15 and No.25 in this year's draft, plus a 2028 second-round pick, in exchange for the seven-time Bombers best and fairest and three-time All Australian.

The midfielder joins Hawthorn on a long-term contract, reportedly worth $4 million over four years with a trigger for a fifth season.

"Zach has long been celebrated as one of the most elite midfielders in the AFL, and he will play a key role in our side for many years to come," Hawthorn list boss Mark McKenzie said.

"His professionalism and competitiveness are second to none."

In 2025, Essendon knocked back Hawthorn's final offer of two first-round picks (10 and 22), a future first-rounder, and now-delisted midfielder Henry Hustwaite.

Bombers president Andrew Welsh had warned Hawthorn not to get "too cute with us again" in an interview with the Herald Sun.

McKenzie said the Hawks had learned after waiting until about 30 hours before the 2025 trade deadline to make first contact with Essendon about Merrett.

Merrett, who was entering the final year of his contract, stepped down as Essendon captain but featured in all 23 matches on his way to securing a seventh Crichton Medal.

Essendon paid tribute to the 274-gamer as the defining Bomber of his generation.

"When people look back on this era of Essendon, Zach's name will be one of the first they mention," Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said.

With the Merrett deal done, Hawthorn's attention will turn to acquiring Gold Coast key forward Ben King as a restricted free agent.

The Hawks are expected to lodge paperwork for King on Tuesday, with the Suns afforded three days to match their contract offer.

Gold Coast list boss Kall Burns said the Suns would take their time to consider whether to match or accept band one compensation, currently valued at pick No.7.

"You've got to weigh up what you can possibly get in if it's a trade," he said.

"It is only day one of the trade period."

Hawthorn fell at the preliminary final hurdle for a second straight year, losing to eventual premiers Brisbane by nine points.

stories.headline: USMNT's young stars shine to give Pochettino 'fantastic problem'
stories.summary: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.
stories.body:
GLENDALE, Ariz. -- United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.

The U.S. endured a difficult first half, and scored completely against the run of play in the 28th minute when Hall converted from close range after Mexico keeper Raúl Rangel spilled Gio Reyna's low cross right in front of goal.

- Cavan Sullivan has arrived: U.S. phenom's goal caps a memorable win over Mexico

- Márquez bemoans 'terrible mistakes' as Mexico humbled by USMNT

- USMNT player ratings: Sullivan, Hall 9/10 in big win vs. Mexico

The USMNT began to make more headway in the second half, and doubled its lead in the 62nd minute when Sullivan intercepted a pass from Rangel, and chipped the ball into the net from 35 yards out. The match lost its edge when Mexico's Mateo Chávez was red carded in the 67th minute following a scrap with Sebastian Berhalter.

Malik Tillman finished off the scoring in the 84th minute, latching onto another wayward Mexico pass to firing into the net.

Hall, 18, is just the third USMNT player to score in his first three national team appearances, while 17-year-old Sullivan became the youngest scorer in USMNT history.

"I think it's a fantastic problem for us," Pochettino said about the performances of his team's young players. "I think we will take the right decision in the right moment, but I think it's a very good problem to see.

"Now it's not a moment at all, but yes, we appreciate that situation and of course hope that we will be in that situation that young players perform in the way that they deserve to be with us."

Pochettino also pronounced himself pleased with the way his side weathered Mexico's early pressure.

"I think that this, overall, was a great opportunity to discover ourself, to see ourselves in a difficult game with a very good team. Again, Mexico is a great team," Pochettino said.

"Yes, I think two different maybe halves. The first half I think Mexico started really well. They forced us to play back. We never connected. We were losing all the duels. And then we start to grow after 15, 20 minutes. And I think it was a good lesson the first half because it was the sense of work all together, suffer together even when you are not playing well in the way that you plan to play."

But Pochettino couldn't help but admire the performance of Sullivan, who impressed with his work on both sides the ball.

"I think he's a talented player with enormous quality, but with a very good balance, in possession and out of possession," Pochettino said about Sullivan. "He's a fighter, he's a warrior. It's difficult to find this type of player with a tremendous quality.

"And then I think Cavan showed in possession with the ball on the field [and] when he need to be chasing people and recover the ball. That is my impression after maybe three weeks together. And that is unbelievable, to have a player like this. I think it's a fantastic news for USA. Hope that continues in that way."

Pochettino was careful to laud Sullivan's young teammates as well, who have largely impressed during this window.

"It's a big moment because we need to be right with them," Pochettino said about the win, and the path forward. "We need to protect them. We need to support them. Our responsibility now is that this group of talented players grow in the right direction."

stories.headline: UEFA receives Real Madrid dossier on Barcelona-Negreira case
stories.summary: UEFA has received "a substantial amount of documents" from Real Madrid related to its ongoing inquiry into the Negreira case, European football's governing body said on Thursday.
stories.body:
MADRID -- UEFA has received "a substantial amount of documents" from Real Madrid related to its ongoing inquiry into the Negreira case, European football's governing body said on Thursday.

Payments made by Barcelona to companies linked to José María Enriquez Negreira -- the former vice-president of Spain's Technical Committee of Referees -- over two decades have been subject to a UEFA investigation since 2023, while there is also an ongoing Spanish criminal case.

Barcelona have said the payments, which totaled over €7 million ($7.9m), were made for technical refereeing reports.

- Ronaldo's Portugal walkout is nothing new; he has a long history of rows with coaches

- Source: Mbappé to be available for Clásico

- Raphinha back at Barça, injured in Brazil game

"UEFA can confirm that it has received from Real Madrid CF a substantial amount of documents related to the ongoing investigation into FC Barcelona in the matter involving José María Enríquez Negreira," UEFA confirmed in a statement on Thursday.

"The UEFA Ethics and Disciplinary Inspectors have also received these latest documents which they will assess as part of their ongoing review."

Real Madrid said the dossier included "extensive documentation and evidence regarding events of extraordinary seriousness, which directly affect the integrity of the competition and confidence in the refereeing system."

"Real Madrid C.F. considers it essential that, now that UEFA has this documentation, the investigation proceeds with the utmost urgency until its full conclusion, and that the competent bodies take the appropriate decisions in accordance with the severity of the verified facts," the club said.

"Our club will continue to actively collaborate with UEFA and take all actions within its power to clarify events that it deems incompatible with the principles of integrity, transparency, and fair play that should govern European football."

In May, Madrid president Florentino Pérez said that the club was gathering evidence to submit a dossier to UEFA.

Having previously adopted a conciliatory tone with Barcelona -- saying in 2024 that the two clubs "have to help each other" as they worked together on the proposed European Super League -- Pérez has since been extremely critical of his LaLiga rivals.

"They've stolen seven league [titles] from me," Pérez said in May.

In a statement, Barcelona emphasized that Thursday's development did not equate to "any new proceedings."

"The proceedings were initiated in 2023, with the appointment of two investigators who have since carried out the action they deemed appropriate," Barcelona said. "The Club has always complied with all their requests. These proceedings have not been reopened because they have never been closed.

"The UEFA statement confirms receipt of documentation submitted by Real Madrid and indicates that the investigators will assess it within the framework of the existing investigation. The same text expressly refers, on two occasions, to an investigation and a review that are 'ongoing.' It therefore does not announce the opening, reopening, or reactivation of any proceedings, nor does it contain any assessment of the substance or value of the documentation provided.

"It is up to the investigators to determine what action, if any, they consider appropriate regarding this documentation. As of today, they have not made any new requests to FC Barcelona nor have they forwarded Real Madrid's complaint to the Club. Should they do so, the Club will respond accordingly, as it has done up to now.

"In accordance with the applicable legislation governing this matter, these proceedings are subject to the outcome of the criminal case currently being heard in Spain and will continue to be so."

stories.headline: 'The start of something special': Ponga sees hope beyond Knights' Grand Final heartbreak
stories.summary: Kalyn Ponga believes Newcastle's remarkable return to the Grand Final can be "the start of something special", but has warned the Knights will have to earn their opportunity all over again.
stories.body:
Kalyn Ponga believes Newcastle's remarkable return to the Grand Final can be "the start of something special", but has warned the Knights will have to earn their opportunity all over again.

Speaking to ESPN after the Grand Final loss to the Sydney Roosters, Ponga balanced pride in Newcastle's turnaround with the disappointment of falling short of the premiership.

The Knights' rise from wooden spooners to grand finalists has given their captain reason to believe in the club's future. It has also reinforced how much a title would mean to the community they represent.

"We obviously know the responsibility that we have as players representing this proud community, and this year, I think we've done that well," Ponga said.

"I do feel like this is the start of something special for this club and this community.

"They deserve a premiership. They deserve to be winning."

The defeat was still raw when Ponga reflected on a season that transformed Newcastle's fortunes.

While the ending was painful, it did not erase the enjoyment he had taken from the journey or his pride in the group.

"Oh man, I've enjoyed so much of it," he said.

"Yeah, it is hard, but hopefully for this group, this club and this town, it's only the beginning. There is so much to look forward to.

"I think the youth that's coming through is exciting, but at the same token, nothing's given. You've got to earn everything again.

"I'm so proud of this season, for sure."

That warning was a recurring theme in Ponga's assessment. Newcastle have given themselves a foundation to build on, but their captain is conscious that one Grand Final appearance guarantees little about the next campaign.

Asked what gave him confidence the Knights could continue competing for premierships, Ponga pointed to the club's position, the hunger of its established players and the emerging talent around them.

"I think the club's in a good position," he said.

"It takes a good club to win games and put yourselves in positions to win.

"We're still hungry. The ultimate prize is to win a comp, and there's a lot in this group who haven't done that.

"But there's a lot of boys in this group that have been here for a long time and want it so bad."

For Ponga, the combination of those experienced players and youngsters still at the beginning of their NRL careers offers encouragement.

"You sprinkle in some of the youth that's coming through -- 20-year-olds that have played 10 games, 21-year-olds, 22-year-olds -- it is exciting," he said.

"I just don't want to get lost through it, though. We've got to work hard."

Ponga was equally measured when asked whether the loss could become a catalyst for sustained success, as Penrith's 2020 Grand Final defeat preceded their run of premierships.

He resisted drawing a parallel with Nathan Cleary and the Panthers.

"It's hard to compare," Ponga said.

"What Nath's done and that Penrith club has done is remarkable. It's hard to compare this position.

"At the moment, we're just a team that's lost a Grand Final.

"Like I said, there is a lot to look forward to, but it's hard to look past that."

There was no attempt to rush beyond the disappointment. The hope was there, but so was an understanding of the work required to turn it into something more.

Ponga's final message was for the supporters who had followed Newcastle through the turnaround.

"I just want to say thank you for the support," he said. "It's been unreal."
